judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate File 473, which bars the state from ruling out a foster or adoptive parent because of that person's religious or moral beliefs about sexual orientation or gender identity. The health and human services department may not require a foster parent, a kinship caregiver or a prospective adoptive parent to affirm or support a policy on those subjects that conflicts with those beliefs. It also may not refuse to license or approve someone, or rule the person out as a placement, on that ground. That protection covers a stated intent to raise a child in line with those beliefs. The Iowa House passed it 58-34, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 2711, which removes affirmative action from Iowa law. It strikes the state's policy of applying affirmative action to correct problems in state hiring, along with the affirmative action plans and reports required of state agencies, the board of regents, the judicial branch, school districts, area education agencies and community colleges. Similar requirements for the law enforcement academy and the board of medicine also go. The bar on denying anyone a public job because of race, creed, color, religion, national origin, sex, age or disability stays in place. The Iowa Senate passed it 31-15, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 928, which rewrites how Iowa recounts and contests elections. A candidate for statewide or federal office may demand a recount only when the margin is under fifteen hundredths of one percent, and a legislative candidate only when it is under one percent or fifty votes, whichever is smaller. The recount then covers every precinct where a vote was cast for the office. Recount boards must follow the secretary of state's written guidance. The secretary may stop a county recount, take custody of the ballots and equipment, run the recount with state staff, and fine a county elections commissioner up to twenty-five thousand dollars for deliberately breaking the rules. The Iowa House passed it 66-31, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 767, which changes Iowa's private sector drug testing law in employers' favor. A safety-sensitive job, where an employer may test at random, is now any job the employer designates as one where an accident could kill or seriously injure someone, rather than a job that in fact fits that description. Employers may hand over test results in person or send them electronically if the worker agrees, instead of only by certified mail. The act also narrows who can be sued for breaking the law from any person to the employer alone. The Iowa House passed it 60-32, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 2329, which raises the interest that licensed lenders may charge on regulated loans. Iowa capped the rate on a sliding scale that fell as the balance grew, from three percent a month on the first one hundred fifty dollars to one percent a month on any balance over seven hundred dollars. The act strikes that scale and sets one cap of three percent a month on the whole balance. It also changes the service charge on a consumer credit transaction from the lesser of ten percent of the amount financed or thirty dollars to the lesser of three percent or one hundred dollars. The Iowa Senate passed it 34-11, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate File 304, which takes away a minor's ability to get a vaccine against a sexually transmitted infection without a parent's consent. Iowa law lets a minor consent alone to care for preventing, diagnosing or treating a sexually transmitted disease, and the act carves vaccination out of that rule. Testing and treatment still need no parental consent. The Iowa House passed it 63-29, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate File 383, which regulates pharmacy benefit managers, the firms that run drug coverage for health plans. They may not pay an Iowa retail pharmacy less than the published national average cost of buying the drug, and may not pay an independent pharmacy less than they pay a pharmacy they own. They may not steer a patient toward a particular pharmacy through copays or reimbursement, shut a willing pharmacy out of a network, or impose accreditation terms beyond state licensing rules. The act also sets contract rules and an appeals process for pharmacies. The Iowa Senate passed it 36-14, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate File 2422, which tightens eligibility rules for food assistance and Medicaid. The health and human services department must check applicants against a federal immigration and citizenship database, report food assistance payment error rates to the legislature every quarter, and ask Washington to let it wipe unused food benefits after about three months instead of nine. Retroactive Medicaid coverage is cut to at most two months before the application for pregnant women, children and nursing home residents, and the department is barred from seeking any waiver to go further back. Unless the legislature approves, the department may not seek Medicaid waivers or plan changes that raise net spending or expand coverage, with exceptions for changes federal law requires, settlements of federal Medicaid violations, and managed-care payment rates. The Iowa Senate passed it 27-16, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 2501, which makes several changes to how Iowa runs elections. Police and other agencies must tell the secretary of state at once when they investigate an election, an election official or suspected election misconduct. County auditors must cancel a voter registration that has sat incomplete or unconfirmed for ninety days when they cannot reach the voter or the voter does not fix the problem. All election equipment must carry a tamper-evident seal at all times, and the act sets when a recount of a ballot question must be held. The Iowa Senate passed it 31-16, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 2254, which bans noncompete clauses at the University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics. The board of regents must adopt a policy barring the hospital from putting a noncompete clause in a contract with a doctor, physician assistant, registered nurse, licensed practical nurse, nurse practitioner or pharmacist. A noncompete clause limits where a worker may work after leaving the job, so staff who leave can now keep treating patients nearby. The ban covers contracts signed, renewed or extended after the act took effect. The Iowa House passed it 70-20, and it became law.
